tier_reason: The Are We Fast Yet performance report (suite of the peer-reviewed DLS'16 paper by Marr, Daloze and Mössenböck) shows the record's Graal.js and Node.js geomean, median, sd and max values exactly, so the measured win stays tier B; the report states neither CPU nor flags. The claim is overstated, hence downgrade: the geomean edge comes mostly from one Node.js outlier (Bounce), and the newer, fully reproducible kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023) has Graal.js slower than Node.js on all 13 benchmarks.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Are We Fast Yet performance report (https://github.com/smarr/are-we-fast-yet/blob/master/docs/performance.md, generated 2016-06-20, peak performance after warmup, runtime factor over Java 1.8.0_91, lower is better), geomean: Graal.js 2.23 (median 2.13, sd 2.82, max 12.22) vs Node.js 2.89 (median 2.54, sd 3.33, max 12.25), about 1.3x lower geomean runtime (derived from page data). Per benchmark Graal.js is faster on 8 of 14 (Bounce 1.26 vs 12.25, CD, DeltaBlue, List, NBody, Richards, Storage, Towers), slower on 5 (Havlak 12.22 vs 10.24, Json 1.60 vs 1.14, Mandelbrot, Permute 3.06 vs 2.13, Queens) and tied on Sieve (3.61). Excluding the Bounce outlier the geomeans are 2.33 vs 2.58, about 1.11x (derived from page data). Counter-evidence: kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28, AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, https://github.com/kostya/jit-benchmarks) has Graal.js 22.3.1 (graalnode, node 16.18.1), native and JVM modes, slower than Node.js 19.7.0 on all 13 benchmarks (e.g. brainfuck 76.16 s native / 52.08 s JVM vs 5.88 s, nbody 4.82 / 5.59 vs 0.82, regexdna 10.0 / 6.68 vs 1.06, matmul 0.51 / 0.30 vs 0.26).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: AWFY report: Java 1.8.0_91 baseline; Graal.js and Node.js versions and flags not stated on the page (the DLS'16 paper used Node.js 6.2, per a search snippet). kostya/jit-benchmarks: graalnode 22.3.1 (node 16.18.1) vs nodejs 19.7.0, run commands in tools/languages.rb, Docker images in docker/.
corrections.caveats: The only measured win is from June 2016 (early Graal.js vs Node.js 6.2), and its geomean edge is driven by Bounce, where Node.js was 12.25x Java; without Bounce the gap is about 1.11x. Node.js is still faster on 5 of 14 AWFY benchmarks (Graal.js has the better median, 2.13 vs 2.54). The independent, reproducible kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023) shows Graal.js 22.3.1 slower than Node.js 19.7.0 on all 13 benchmarks, often by 2x to 13x, so current Graal.js should not be presented as faster than V8. Peak performance only; startup and warmup, where Graal.js is known to be weak, are excluded. The AWFY report states no CPU. The community distribution is UPL-1.0 but Oracle's non-community builds are under the GraalVM Free Terms and Conditions.

tier_reason: The AWFY performance report (suite of the peer-reviewed DLS'16 paper) shows the record's JRuby+Truffle and Node.js values exactly, and kostya/benchmarks (Intel Xeon E-2324G, versions listed, public Docker harness) shows the bench.b numbers exactly, so the evidence stays tier B. The claim is overstated, hence downgrade: TruffleRuby beats Node.js on only 6 of 14 AWFY benchmarks, and beats LuaJIT and PyPy on only 1 of 6 shared kostya/benchmarks tests. The two kostya suites are A-level reproducible but mostly show it slower, so they cannot support an A-tier 'faster' claim.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Are We Fast Yet (https://github.com/smarr/are-we-fast-yet/blob/master/docs/performance.md, 2016-06-20, peak performance, runtime factor over Java 1.8.0_91) 'JRuby+Truffle' (the former name of TruffleRuby): geomean 2.36 (sd 0.94, median 2.64, max 4.31) vs Node.js 2.89 (sd 3.33, median 2.54, max 12.25), about 1.22x lower geomean (derived from page data). It is faster than Node.js on only 6 of 14 benchmarks (Bounce 1.41 vs 12.25, DeltaBlue, Havlak 4.31 vs 10.24, NBody, Richards, Sieve 1.62 vs 3.61), and without the Bounce outlier the geomeans are 2.46 vs 2.58, about 1.05x (derived from page data); Node.js has the better median. Its clear AWFY win is over other Rubies: JRuby 12.83 and MRI 45.62. kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks, update 2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G): on bench.b, truffleruby 34.0.1 native 5.169 s and JVM 4.645 s beat Lua/luajit 5.686 s and Python/pypy 9.398 s (Node.js 2.954 s is faster). On the other shared tests it is slower: mandel.b 48.381 s vs luajit 31.804 s and pypy 41.153 s; Json 10.618 s vs pypy 0.606 s; Matmul 17.667 s vs pypy 3.263 s; Primes 0.871 s vs luajit 0.309 s and pypy 0.617 s. On Base64 the JVM mode ties PyPy (3.505 s vs 3.534 s). kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28, AMD Ryzen 7 3800X): truffleruby 22.3.1 in JVM mode beats PyPy3 7.3.11 on 6 of 13 benchmarks and LuaJIT 2.1.0-beta3 on 5 of 11, for example binarytrees 0.69 s vs 3.84 s (PyPy) and 6.73 s (LuaJIT), and nbody 0.85 s vs 4.44 s and 1.44 s.
corrections.caveats: Mixed against every listed baseline. On AWFY the geomean edge over Node.js comes mostly from Node's Bounce outlier, and Node.js has the better median. On kostya/benchmarks TruffleRuby is slower than LuaJIT and PyPy on 4 of the 6 shared tests (mandel.b, Json, Matmul, Primes), with Matmul 5.4x and Json 17x slower than PyPy. Node.js beats it on every kostya test shown. On kostya/jit-benchmarks 2023 it wins about half the time. AWFY numbers date from 2016, and the paper is co-authored by Benoit Daloze, a TruffleRuby developer, so it is peer-reviewed but not independent. JVM mode has high memory use (about 350 MB base RSS on kostya). plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2) lists Ruby only on the proprietary 'Graal EE 23.1.1' build. The README claim ('fastest Ruby implementation', yjit-bench) compares against other Rubies, not the listed baselines.
